title: Hear, O Israel (Deuteronomy 6:4–9)
hook: love God with all your heart, soul and strength; talk of it at home and on the road

segments.voice: Yesterday, Balaam's donkey, who saw the angel her master couldn't. Your line was even a donkey can see. Whose advice did you take seriously? Day four hundred six, the end of week fifty-eight.

On the doorframes of Jewish homes that keep the custom, on the right side, angled a little, there's a small case, sometimes plain, sometimes beautifully decorated. Some people touch it as they go in and out, and kiss their fingers afterward. Inside the case is a tiny rolled scroll, handwritten. And the words on that scroll are the ones Moses speaks in today's passage. Moses is old now. The people are at the edge of the land, and he's giving them his last long speech, the book of Deuteronomy. In the middle of it comes one word that Jewish prayer still speaks every morning and every night: hear.
screen: `A SMALL CASE ON THE DOORFRAME.` → `A HANDWRITTEN SCROLL INSIDE.` → `MOSES' LAST SPEECH: HEAR.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD: And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might." In Hebrew the first word is shema, hear, and the whole passage takes its name from it. It isn't just listen. It's hear and take it in, hear and do. And then: love. With your heart, the place in Hebrew where you think and decide, not just feel. With your soul, your whole living self. With all your might: the Hebrew word is almost the word very, so some teachers say, with all your muchness. Everything you've got. Then Moses says where this love lives, and the answer is: everywhere ordinary. Teach these words to your children. Talk of them "when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up." At home, on the road, at bedtime, at breakfast. Bind them on your hand and between your eyes. "And thou shalt write them upon the posts of thy house, and on thy gates." That's the case on the doorframe, the mezuzah, a Hebrew word that simply means doorpost. Jews who pray say the Shema morning and evening, and tradition holds it as words for the very end of life too. And Christians hear it too. When a scribe asks Jesus which commandment is first of all, Mark's Gospel says he answers with this one, starting with the very same words: Hear, O Israel. It's been quite a week: Bezalel's hands, the corners of the field, the jubilee horn, the blessing, the spies, the donkey, and now the word on the door.
screen: `SHEMA: HEAR, AND DO.` · `HEART, SOUL, ALL YOUR MUCHNESS.` · `AT HOME, ON THE ROAD, AT BEDTIME.` · `MEZUZAH: THE DOORPOST.` · then, large: `HEAR, O ISRAEL: THE LORD OUR GOD IS ONE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say it at your door. Settle, and breathe, and picture your own front door, the one you walk through every day without noticing. Imagine pausing there. If you pray, you can say the first line, Hear, O Israel, the LORD our God is one LORD, or the words Jesus quoted, as you cross the threshold. If not, choose one thing you love with all your heart, and let the doorway remind you of it. Then picture all the ordinary places the passage names: sitting at home, walking, lying down, getting up. The bell holds the time.
Shema. Hebrew for hear. The first word of Deuteronomy six, four, said morning and evening, and the commandment Jesus called first of all.

Your line: on your doorposts. Today, pause once at a doorway and remember what you love most. And that's week fifty-eight: Bezalel, the edges, jubilee, the blessing, the spies, the donkey, and the Shema. Day four hundred six.

howItsDone: Observant Jews recite the Shema morning and evening and fix a mezuzah to their doorposts; Christians know it as the first great commandment Jesus quoted, and some say it in daily prayer.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old Jewish prayer.
what it means: hear, and love God with everything, everywhere ordinary, at home and on the road and at the door.
what a scholar hears: shema, hear-and-obey; me'od, might, almost 'very'; and Mark 12:29, where Jesus quotes it as first of all.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer opens 'Walk down a street in a Jewish neighborhood' (a banned 'walk into' opener) and no longer generalizes about 'many front doors'; 'all your muchness' framed as a teachers' gloss; 'many hope it will be the last words they say' changed to 'tradition holds'; Shema practice attributed to Jews who pray / observant Jews rather than all Jewish people.
Week fifty-eight counted as days 400–406; confirm.

Mezuzah practice: placed on the right doorpost, angled, containing Deuteronomy 6:4–9 and 11:13–21 handwritten. The script says 'the words Moses speaks in today's passage'; the scroll also contains Deut 11:13–21. Confirm the simplification.
Me'od ('might') as 'muchness': the word is ordinarily the adverb 'very'; this is a common teaching gloss. Confirm it's not a preacher's etymology.
Heart (lev) as the seat of thought and decision: standard. Confirm.
The Shema as hoped-for last words: a widespread Jewish custom; stated as 'many hope'. Confirm.
The practice invites saying Deuteronomy 6:4 at the door 'if you pray'; it is a Jewish prayer text and appears here as scripture Christians share. Keeper to confirm this is respectful.
